summary: This experimental document specifies Depth-First Forwarding (DFF) for IPv6 networks, a forwarding mechanism that can improve delivery reliability in networks with changing topology or lossy links. It works in the forwarding plane, using a method similar to depth-first search for the destination, and can inform the routing plane of failures or loops.

plainLanguage.summary: When a path is blocked, the packet backs up and tries another way, like exploring a maze until it finds the exit.

subtitle: Forwarding packets through alternate paths when the direct route fails, for unreliable networks

tldr.problem: In networks with lossy links or rapidly changing topology, routing tables quickly become stale, causing packets to be dropped even though alternate paths exist. Frequent routing updates consume scarce radio bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: When a packet cannot be delivered through its first-choice neighbor, DFF treats the forwarding decision like a depth-first search: it systematically tries alternate neighbors until one accepts and forwards the packet. Routers track which neighbors have been tried to avoid loops.
tldr.outcome: Packets find alternate paths without waiting for routing protocol updates, improving delivery reliability in dynamic wireless and wired networks with lossy links.

today: RFC 6971 is an Experimental protocol describing DFF as a forwarding mechanism for networks with dynamic topology and lossy links. It has not been obsoleted and remains a reference for experimental implementations in LoWPANs and other low-power wireless mesh networks.

sections.title: Overview: When Routing Fails
sections.content:
Depth-First Forwarding (DFF) is a forwarding mechanism that adapts to rapid topology changes and lossy links by trying alternate paths when the primary path fails. Unlike traditional routing, which relies on a precomputed routing table, DFF makes forwarding decisions in real time at each hop.

In networks with lossy links (wireless mesh networks, underwater acoustic networks, low-power personal area networks), a routing protocol cannot keep the routing table perfectly accurate. More frequent updates worsen the problem by consuming scarce bandwidth and energy. DFF sidesteps this by having each router adaptively try different neighbors when a packet cannot be delivered to the first choice.

DFF works in two modes: route-over (IPv6 routing across multiple hops) and mesh-under (link-layer forwarding within a Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network using LoWPAN). The mechanism is identical in both modes; only the header format and address types differ. DFF is suitable for networks with multiple paths between source and destination and is designed for unicast, low-traffic scenarios with good link-layer acknowledgment support.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of using a map (routing table), the router asks itself: 'Can I send this to neighbor A? No. Neighbor B? No. Neighbor C? Yes!' This works even if the map is out of date.

sections.title: Core Concepts: The Processed Set and Packet State
sections.content:
When a router forwards a packet, it creates or updates a Processed Tuple, a record storing the packet's originator address, sequence number, the previous hop, and a list of neighbors already tried. This Processed Set lets routers detect loops: if a packet arrives again with the same originator and sequence number, the router knows it has been here before.

Each packet has two flags in its DFF header: the Return (RET) flag and the Duplicate (DUP) flag. When a router has tried all its neighbors and none accepted the packet, it sets RET=1 and returns the packet to the previous hop, which continues trying other neighbors. If the packet is returned to the originating router and all neighbors have been tried, the packet is dropped.

The DUP flag is set when a link-layer transmission to a neighbor fails (no acknowledgment received). This marks the packet as possibly duplicated in the network, since the neighbor might have received it despite the missing acknowledgment. DUP helps distinguish between genuine loops and duplicate transmissions; a router receiving a packet with DUP=1 that it has seen before will forward it anyway, while a packet with DUP=0 that has looped is returned.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router remembers which neighbors it already sent the packet to. If a packet comes back, the router tries the next neighbor. A flag marks packets that might be duplicates because an earlier transmission maybe succeeded even though the confirmation was lost.

sections.title: How DFF Forwards Packets
sections.content:
When a new packet enters the DFF domain (either generated locally or arriving from outside), the originating router adds a DFF header with DUP=0, RET=0, and a new sequence number. It then selects a candidate list of next-hop neighbors, preferring those listed in the routing table toward the destination, then other symmetric neighbors.

The router tries the first neighbor. If the link-layer acknowledges delivery, the packet has advanced. If transmission fails (no link-layer ACK within a timeout), the router sets DUP=1 and tries the next neighbor on the list.

If a neighbor receives the packet and cannot forward it further (all its neighbors have been tried), the neighbor returns it with RET=1. The previous hop, upon receiving a returned packet, sets RET=0 and tries the next neighbor on its list.

A parameter MAX_HOP_LIMIT bounds the number of forwards to prevent wasteful detours. Another parameter, P_HOLD_TIME, determines how long a Processed Tuple is retained; it must be long enough for the packet to traverse the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The router makes a list of neighbors, tries the first one. If it fails, try the second, then the third. When a neighbor can't deliver it, the packet comes back and the first router tries another neighbor.

sections.title: IPv6 Route-Over and LoWPAN Mesh-Under Modes
sections.content:
In route-over mode, DFF is implemented as an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options header extension. The header contains the 2-bit version field (set to 00), the DUP and RET flags, and a 16-bit sequence number. This mode applies to general IPv6 networks.

In mesh-under mode, DFF follows the LoWPAN Mesh Addressing header as specified in RFC 4944. The DFF header precedes any header compression or fragmentation headers. Both modes use the same sequence number and flag mechanisms but with different header formats.

For route-over, addresses are IPv6 addresses, the Hop Limit field is the IPv6 Hop Limit, and the Next Hop is resolved to a link-layer address via Neighbor Discovery. For mesh-under, addresses are 16-bit short or 64-bit EUI-64 link-layer addresses, and the Hop Limit corresponds to the 'Deep Hops Left' field in the Mesh Addressing header.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 networks use one kind of header, and low-power wireless networks use another. The forwarding logic is the same; only the addresses and headers are different.

sections.title: Scope Limitations and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
DFF is intended for use within a single routing domain and must not leak beyond it. Routers at the boundary between DFF and non-DFF domains must remove the DFF header when forwarding packets out and add one when receiving packets from outside.

DFF is most suited to networks with multiple redundant paths (mesh topologies) where depth-first search can find alternate routes. Networks with only single paths to some destinations, or networks that can be partitioned by the failure of a single router, are less suitable because packets may exhaust the Hop Limit while exploring dead ends.

DFF scales to networks with moderate traffic (packets per second depend on router memory and loss rate). Each recently forwarded packet requires storage for its sequence number and the list of tried neighbors. Very high traffic or very deep searches can exhaust memory, and if sequence numbers wrap around before old packets leave the network, collision and false positives are possible.

Because DFF is experimental, deployments are encouraged in the applicability domain (LoWPANs and similar small, dynamic networks) and implementations should report performance metrics: optimal P_HOLD_TIME and MAX_HOP_LIMIT values for their network, how DFF interacts with different routing protocols, and whether DFF can improve delivery reliability in hybrid reactive-proactive routing scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: DFF works best in wireless mesh networks with many paths. It doesn't work well in networks with dead ends where the packet runs out of attempts before finding the destination.
